{{short description|1=Family of curves of the form r^n = a^n cos(nθ)}}
{{Sinusoidal_spirals.svg|250px}}

In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''sinusoidal spirals''' are a family of curves defined by the equation in [[polar coordinates]]

:<math>r^n = a^n \cos(n \theta)\,</math>

where {{mvar|a}} is a nonzero constant and {{mvar|n}} is a [[rational number]] other than 0. With a rotation about the origin, this can also be written

:<math>r^n = a^n \sin(n \theta).\,</math>

The term "spiral" is a misnomer, because they are not actually [[spiral]]s, and often have a flower-like shape. Many well known curves are sinusoidal spirals including:
* [[Hyperbola#Rectangular_hyperbola|Rectangular hyperbola]] ({{math|1=''n'' = &minus;2}})
* [[Line (geometry)|Line]] ({{math|1=''n'' = &minus;1}})
* [[Parabola]] ({{math|1=''n'' = &minus;1/2}})
* [[Tschirnhausen cubic]] ({{math|1=''n'' = &minus;1/3}}) 
* [[Cayley's sextic]] ({{math|1=''n'' = 1/3}})
* [[Cardioid]] ({{math|1=''n'' = 1/2}})
* [[Circle]] ({{math|1=''n'' = 1}})
* [[Lemniscate of Bernoulli]] ({{math|1=''n'' = 2}})

The curves were first studied by [[Colin Maclaurin]].

==Equations==
Differentiating
:<math>r^n = a^n \cos(n \theta)\,</math>
and eliminating ''a'' produces a [[differential equation]] for ''r'' and &theta;:
:<math>\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos n\theta + r\sin n\theta =0. </math>

Then
:<math>\left(\frac{dr}{ds},\ r\frac{d\theta}{ds}\right)\cos n\theta \frac{ds}{d\theta}
= \left(-r\sin n\theta ,\ r \cos n\theta \right)
= r\left(-\sin n\theta ,\ \cos n\theta \right)</math> 
which implies that the polar [[tangential angle]] is 
:<math>\psi = n\theta \pm \pi/2</math> 
and so the tangential angle is 
:<math>\varphi = (n+1)\theta \pm \pi/2. </math>
(The sign here is positive if ''r'' and cos ''n''&theta; have the same sign and negative otherwise.)

The unit tangent vector,
:<math>\left(\frac{dr}{ds},\ r\frac{d\theta}{ds}\right),</math>
has length one, so comparing the magnitude of the vectors on each side of the above equation gives
:<math>\frac{ds}{d\theta} = r \cos^{-1} n\theta = a \cos^{-1+\tfrac{1}{n}} n\theta. </math>
In particular, the length of a single loop when <math>n>0</math> is:
:<math>a\int_{-\tfrac{\pi}{2n}}^{\tfrac{\pi}{2n}} \cos^{-1+\tfrac{1}{n}} n\theta\ d\theta</math>
The substitution <math>r=\cos^{\tfrac{1}{n}}(n\theta)</math> induces the
transformation
:<math>\int_{0}^{\tfrac{\pi}{2n}} \cos^{-1+\tfrac{1}{n}} n\theta\ d\theta=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-r^{2n}}}</math>
Hence the length of a single loop of the spiral may be reexpressed as:
:<math>2a \int_{0}^{1}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-r^{2n}}}</math>
The [[curvature]] is given by
:<math>\frac{d\varphi}{ds} = (n+1)\frac{d\theta}{ds} = \frac{n+1}{a} \cos^{1-\tfrac{1}{n}} n\theta. </math>

==Properties==
The [[Inverse curve|inverse]] of a sinusoidal spiral with respect to a circle with center at the origin is another sinusoidal spiral whose value of ''n'' is the negative of the original curve's value of ''n''. For example, the inverse of the lemniscate of Bernoulli is a rectangular hyperbola.

The [[isoptic]], [[pedal curve|pedal]] and negative pedal of a sinusoidal spiral are different sinusoidal spirals.

One path of a particle moving according to a [[central force]] proportional to a power of ''r'' is a sinusoidal spiral.

When <math>n</math> is a positive integer, the sinusoidal spiral <math>r^n=\cos(n\theta)</math> can be described as follows. Let <math>n</math> points be arranged symmetrically on a circle of radius <math>\frac{a}{2^{\frac{1}{n}}}</math> centered at the origin with one point on the positive <math>x</math>-axis. Then the set of points, so that the product of the distances from that point to these <math>n</math> points is <math>\frac{a^n}{2}</math>, is precisely this sinusoidal spiral. Consequenly the sinusoidal spiral can be identified with the set of complex numbers <math>z</math> satisfying the equation <math>\left|z^n-\frac{a^n}{2}\right|=\frac{a^n}{2}</math>. Thus such a spiral is a [[polynomial lemniscate]].
